notes: Ruling slot 0 = PPT (sole legal party since 1962). Chad had no real coalition partner; slot 13 holds the French-led Administrative Reform Mission (MRA, 1969), the technocratic body co-governing the north. FROLINAT leadership in 7 (Libya/Sudan-backed), First Army in 5, Toubou Second Army in 6, UNT left wing in 19.

0.name: Parti Progressiste Tchadien
0.text:
The Chadian Progressive Party, the Chadian section of the African Democratic Rally (RDA), was founded in 1947 and has ruled since independence in 1960. Under President François Tombalbaye, its leader since 1959, it became the sole legal party in 1962, and its political bureau is dominated by southern Sara cadres.

The party is firmly pro-French: French troops have been fighting alongside the national army against the northern rebellion since 1968, and Paris funds much of the budget. It promises national unity and development but rules through purges, arrests and patronage. Its strength lies in the civil service, the cotton-growing south and French military protection, while its hold on the Muslim north is collapsing.

1.name: Archidiocèse de Fort-Lamy
1.text:
The Archdiocese of Fort-Lamy heads the Catholic Church in Chad, raised to an archdiocese in 1961 under the French Jesuit Archbishop Paul Dalmais. Its missions, schools and dispensaries are concentrated in the south among the Sara, Moundang and Ngambaye, and have trained much of the educated elite that now staffs the state, Tombalbaye's party included.

The Church favours order, the protection of Christian education, rural development cooperatives and close ties to France and the Western world. It is uneasy about the regime's growing arbitrariness and fears that the northern rebellion could become a religious war. Its leverage lies in its schools, the moral authority of its priests in southern villages and Catholic aid from Europe.

2.name: Les Amis de Lisette
2.text:
Les Amis de Lisette are the surviving loyalists of Gabriel Lisette, the Panamanian-born colonial administrator of Guadeloupean origin who founded the Chadian Progressive Party in 1947 and served as the territory's first head of government. Tombalbaye pushed him aside and in 1960 barred his return while he was abroad; he now lives in France.

His friends, mostly older évolués, civil servants and graduates of the colonial schools, advocate pluralism, an independent judiciary, the restoration of civil liberties and a negotiated settlement with the northern rebels. They are pro-Western and francophile. Their leverage lies in their contacts in Paris and among French officials, who sometimes see them as a reserve team for a Chad after Tombalbaye.

3.name: Mouvement Socialiste Africain
3.text:
The African Socialist Movement in Chad was the local branch of the interterritorial party linked to the French SFIO, built in the 1950s by Ahmed Koulamallah, a Baguirmian notable and religious leader. Banned with all other parties in 1962, it was broken in the crackdown of 1963, when Koulamallah was arrested; its sympathizers survive among the Muslims of Fort-Lamy and the Chari-Baguirmi.

Its programme is democratic socialism in the French tradition: multiparty government, trade-union rights, public education and fair representation of Muslims and northerners. It remains pro-Western and seeks reconciliation rather than war. Its leverage lies in memories of Koulamallah's popularity in the capital and among moderate Muslim notables.

4.name: Fédération des étudiants d'Afrique noire en France
4.english: Federation of Black African Students in France
4.native_full: Fédération des étudiants d'Afrique noire en France
4.text:
The Federation of Black African Students in France, founded in 1950, is the radical umbrella of African students in France, and its Chadian section gathers the few hundred scholarship holders studying in Paris, Bordeaux and other cities. Hostile to Tombalbaye and to the French military intervention, it publishes resolutions condemning the regime and keeps contacts with the rebel front and Soviet-bloc embassies.

Its members embrace Marxism-Leninism: they demand the withdrawal of French troops, nationalization of the cotton trade, land reform, a democratic state for northerners and southerners alike and alignment with the socialist camp. Their leverage is small but real, since the regime depends on precisely these graduates to staff ministries, schools and hospitals.
4.wiki: Federation of Black African Students in France

5.name: Première armée de libération du FROLINAT
5.native_full: Première armée de libération du FROLINAT
5.text:
The First Liberation Army is the main fighting force of the National Liberation Front of Chad in the centre and east, active in Ouaddaï, Batha, Guéra and Salamat. Its guerrilla bands grew out of the 1965 tax revolt at Mangalmé and were organized by Ibrahim Abatcha, killed in combat in February 1968; since 1969 they have faced French troops and aircraft.

Its commanders, mostly Arabic-speaking villagers and veterans of the Sudanese army, uphold Abatcha's radical line: overthrow of the neo-colonial regime, expulsion of French troops, an end to exactions by southern officials and chiefs, and a socialist Chad. They take aid from Sudan and Libya. Their leverage is control of rural districts the government no longer dares enter.

6.name: Deuxième armée de libération du FROLINAT
6.native_full: Deuxième armée de libération du FROLINAT
6.text:
The Second Liberation Army is the rebel force of Borkou-Ennedi-Tibesti, made up largely of Toubou warriors who rose in 1968 after the nomad guards at Aozou mutinied against southern administrators. Formally part of the National Liberation Front, it is led by Toubou clan chiefs and young commanders such as Goukouni Oueddei, son of the exiled Derde of the Tibesti.

It fights less for socialism than for the honour, autonomy and customary law of the Toubou, the return of the Derde and the expulsion of southern officials and French troops. It is anti-Western and leans on Libya for shelter and arms. Its leverage is its mastery of the desert and of the Libyan border.

7.name: Front de Libération Nationale du Tchad
7.native_full: Front de Libération Nationale du Tchad
7.text:
The National Liberation Front of Chad was founded in June 1966 at Nyala in Sudan by exiles led by Ibrahim Abatcha, uniting the Chadian National Union with Muslim dissidents of the north and east. After Abatcha's death in 1968, Dr Abba Siddick, a former minister of Tombalbaye, has emerged as secretary-general, directing the front from abroad while its armies fight inside the country.

FROLINAT wants the overthrow of Tombalbaye, the withdrawal of French troops, equality for Muslims and northerners, the promotion of Arabic and a revolutionary, anti-imperialist government. It draws arms and sanctuary from Sudan and from Gaddafi's new Libyan republic. Its leverage lies in a rebellion that now covers most of the north and east.

8.name: Les Libanais de Fort-Lamy
8.text:
Les Libanais de Fort-Lamy are the small Lebanese merchant community of the capital and Moundou, many of them Shia from South Lebanon who arrived through French West and Equatorial Africa. They run import firms, cloth shops and transport companies and keep a low profile under a regime suspicious of foreign traders.

Their notables follow the reformist leadership of Imam Musa al-Sadr in Beirut, who calls for social justice and dignity for Lebanon's Shia, and favour a moderate, educated Shi'ism. Politically they seek protection of property, good relations with whoever governs and neutrality between the blocs. Their leverage lies in credit, imports and their role as middlemen between French firms and African traders.

9.name: Les Disciples de Najaf
9.text:
Les Disciples de Najaf are a few young Lebanese Shia in Fort-Lamy and Moundou who have studied, or have relatives studying, at the seminaries of Najaf in Iraq, where the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini teaches. They gather in private prayer meetings and challenge the cautious, commercial piety of their elders.

They believe clerics should lead the community in public life, condemn the Shah of Iran and Western domination of Muslim lands, and want stricter observance of Shia law in the diaspora. They have no wider following in Chad and no organization worth the name. Their leverage is the money of a few traders and the authority of clerics visiting from Lebanon and Iraq.

10.name: al-Tariqa al-Tijaniyya
10.text:
The Tijaniyya is the dominant Sufi brotherhood among the Muslims of Chad, with its lodges in Abéché, Fort-Lamy, Massenya and the Kanem and its leading sheikhs tied to the old sultanates and to Islamic teachers in northern Nigeria and Sudan. Its ulama run Quranic schools and preside over Islamic courts for personal and family matters.

Its sheikhs preach obedience to legitimate authority and have largely stayed out of the rebellion, but they protest discrimination against Muslims in the administration and the neglect of Arabic. They want Islamic courts respected, Arabic taught in state schools and Muslim notables given a greater role. Their leverage is their mediation between the regime and rebellious Muslim communities.

11.name: Les Ansar du Ouaddaï
11.text:
Les Ansar du Ouaddaï are the Chadian followers of the Sudanese Mahdiyya, the movement founded by Muhammad Ahmad al-Mahdi in the 1880s, whose descendants lead the Ansar sect in Sudan. Their networks run through Masalit, Arab and Ouaddaian communities straddling the border, and some of their young men carry arms in the rebellion.

They see the struggle against Tombalbaye as a holy war against an infidel state and call for an Islamic order under sharia uniting the Muslims on both sides of the border. They reject both Western and Soviet patrons. Their leverage lies in religious zeal, cross-border kinship and the support of Ansar notables in Darfur.

12.name: Les Frères d'Abéché
12.text:
Les Frères d'Abéché are young Chadian Muslims educated at Al-Azhar in Cairo and in Khartoum, where they encountered the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood of Hassan al-Turabi. Back in Abéché and Fort-Lamy, they teach in Franco-Arab schools and private Quranic academies and meet in reading circles beyond the reach of the single party.

They call for an Islamic society reformed from below: Arabic-language schooling, moral renewal, sharia in family and civil law and political rights for Muslims within a representative state. They distrust the Marxists of the rebellion as much as the French. Their leverage lies in schools, mosques and the prestige of Arab learning among northern youth.

13.name: Mission de Réforme Administrative
13.text:
The Administrative Reform Mission was created in 1969 at the insistence of France, which made it a condition of its military intervention. Headed by Pierre Lami, a veteran French colonial administrator, and staffed by French officials seconded to Chadian prefectures, it effectively co-governs the rebel-affected north and east alongside Tombalbaye's officials.

Its programme is pragmatic counter-insurgency: restoring the authority of sultans and canton chiefs, curbing abuses by southern civil servants and tax collectors, reforming customary justice and reopening dialogue with Muslim notables. It is neither ideological nor partisan, but sees itself as the guardian of a functioning state. Its leverage lies in French money and troops and in Tombalbaye's dependence on both.

14.name: Les Chefs de Canton
14.text:
Les Chefs de Canton are the traditional and appointed chiefs who administer Chad's rural cantons, collecting taxes, judging disputes and recruiting labour in the name of the state. Many were humiliated after independence, when party officials overrode them, and the resulting resentment fed the 1965 Mangalmé revolt; the French-led administrative reform is now restoring their powers.

They want respect for customary law and chiefly authority, moderate taxes and an end to arbitrary acts by party officials and soldiers. They are attached to order and to France as the guarantor of their status, but stay outside Cold War politics. Their leverage lies in their control over villages, tax rolls and local justice.

15.name: Compagnie Française pour le Développement des Fibres Textiles
15.english: French Company for the Development of Textile Fibres
15.native_full: Compagnie Française pour le Développement des Fibres Textiles
15.text:
The French Company for the Development of Textile Fibres is the semi-public French firm that organizes Chad's cotton economy, distributing seed, advising growers and supervising the harvest in the Logone and Moyen-Chari. Cotton provides most of the country's exports, and the company, together with the Cotonfran ginning concern, is the real economic power of the south.

It favours stability, compulsory cultivation quotas, low producer prices and close cooperation with the regime and with Paris. It opposes nationalization and resents the party's levies on farmers. Its leverage lies in the export revenues on which the state budget depends and in the expertise no Chadian institution can yet replace.

16.name: Les Négociants du Ouaddaï
16.text:
Les Négociants du Ouaddaï are the Arab, Hausa and Ouaddaian traders who carry cattle, gum arabic, natron and manufactured goods between Abéché, Fort-Lamy, Darfur, Libya and Nigeria. Their caravans and lorries keep the north and east supplied even as the rebellion spreads and government posts close.

They want an end to the arbitrary taxes, customs abuses and forced levies imposed by party officials, free movement of cattle and goods across borders and rules that do not penalize trade with Sudan and Nigeria. Neutral in the Cold War, they deal with both government and rebels. Their leverage lies in their control over food supply and informal credit in the Sahel.

17.name: Les Gardiens du Lac
17.text:
Les Gardiens du Lac are the Buduma fishermen, Kanembu farmers and herders of the shores and islands of Lake Chad, joined by the wildlife wardens of the Zakouma national park in the southeast. Since the late 1960s the rains have weakened, the lake has begun to shrink, and hunting and poaching are thinning the wildlife of the savanna.

They demand protection of the lake's waters and fisheries, controls on hunting and poaching, preservation of grazing land and state attention to a looming drought. Strangers to Cold War politics, they appeal to international agencies and scientists. Their leverage is small, resting on local knowledge and growing alarm about the Sahel.

18.name: Les Syndicats de Fort-Lamy
18.text:
Les Syndicats de Fort-Lamy are the trade unionists of the capital – civil servants, teachers, drivers and employees of French firms – whose unions have been brought under the control of the ruling party. Strikes are forbidden in practice, and union leaders who resisted were arrested in the purges of the 1960s.

They seek an African socialism of fair wages, Africanization of skilled posts, cooperatives for cotton farmers and genuine union independence. They are non-aligned, distrust both the French firms and the rebels, and would back a civilian reform government. Their leverage lies in their ability to paralyse the capital's administration, power station and transport.

19.name: Union Nationale Tchadienne
19.text:
The Chadian National Union was founded in 1958 as the radical, Arab-leaning nationalist party of the Muslim centre and north. Banned in 1962, it survived in exile in Sudan, Ghana and Egypt, where cadres such as Ibrahim Abatcha turned to Marxism and guerrilla war; in 1966 it merged into the National Liberation Front, where it forms the ideological left.

Its members want an independent socialist revolution owing nothing to Moscow or Paris, admire China's people's war, and favour land reform, nationalization and peasant power. They distrust Abba Siddick's diplomatic and Arabist line. Their leverage lies in the commanders and political commissars they provide to the guerrilla armies.

20.name: Les Patriotes du Sud
20.text:
Les Patriotes du Sud are the hard-line southern cadres of the ruling party, mostly Sara officials, teachers and officers who see the northern rebellion as a revival of the Muslim slave raids that devastated the south in the nineteenth century. They dominate party committees in the Moyen-Chari and Logone and fill the posts of prefects and tax collectors in the north.

They demand a war without compromise against the rebels, no concessions to Muslims or Arabic, and a Chad led by the Christian and animist south. They resent French pressure to reform the administration. Their leverage lies in the party apparatus, the army's southern officer corps and the president's own Sara base.

21.name: Les Miliciens du Parti
21.text:
Les Miliciens du Parti are the youth activists and vigilantes of the Chadian Progressive Party who enforce party discipline in Fort-Lamy and the towns of the south, collecting dues, denouncing suspects and harassing traders from the north. They operate alongside the political police in the arrests that have followed every alleged plot since 1963.

They advocate a cult of the leader, total mobilization of the nation behind Tombalbaye and the party, harsh punishment for 'traitors' and the subordination of chiefs, churches and unions to the state. They are anti-communist and anti-Arab. Their leverage lies in intimidation, informers and the protection of the presidency.

22.name: Forces Armées Tchadiennes
22.text:
The Chadian Armed Forces, built from colonial units after 1960 and backed by the National and Nomadic Guard, are fighting a losing war against the northern rebellion. Since 1969 French troops and aircraft have taken over much of the fighting while French officers retrain Chadian battalions. The officer corps is largely southern, and Félix Malloum is among its rising senior commanders.

The officers want resources, professionalism and respect, and are increasingly bitter at being blamed for defeats while party loyalists are promoted. They are pro-French and anti-communist, but resent the president's purges and interference. Their leverage lies in their arms and in the fact that the regime's survival depends on them.

23.name: Sultanat du Ouaddaï
23.text:
The Sultanate of Wadai at Abéché is the most prestigious of Chad's old Muslim monarchies, alongside the sultanate of Baguirmi at Massenya and the Derde of the Tibesti. Its sultans, once masters of a great Sahelian empire, were reduced to ceremonial chiefs under French rule and further humbled after independence by southern administrators.

The sultanate seeks restored authority over justice, land and the Muslim courts, a recognized place for traditional rulers in the state and respect for Islam. It has kept apart from the rebellion while sympathizing with its grievances, and is now courted by the French administrative reform. Its leverage lies in its legitimacy among Ouaddaian clans and the Muslim east.
